title: Jaya Bachchan and Kareena Kapoor Just Rewrote the Rules on the Male Gaze. Bollywood Is Listening.
excerpt: The Peddi controversy forced a reckoning. Jaya recalled the one director she never worked with again. Kareena invoked Sridevi, Kajol, and her own mother-in-law. The director apologized. The re-edit is confirmed.
body:
It started with a costume. A village girl in clothes no village girl would wear. Camera angles that lingered where they shouldn't have. A kiss scene that looked less like romance and more like coercion. And then the conversation exploded.

Ram Charan's blockbuster Peddi, directed by Buchi Babu Sana, has crossed ₹270 crore at the box office in its first week. But the number everyone's actually talking about is zero — as in the number of people in the industry who can pretend they didn't notice how Janhvi Kapoor's character was filmed.

The backlash arrived in waves. First from audiences on social media, using words like hypersexuality, voyeurism, and male gaze with surgical precision. Then from critics who pointed out that Janhvi's Achiyamma — a rural woman — was styled and shot like a music video fantasy, not a character in a story. And then, in a move that turned a trending hashtag into an industry reckoning, two of Bollywood's most powerful women spoke up.

"Nobody Ever Dared to Cross the Line With Me"

In an interview with Deccan Chronicle, Jaya Bachchan was characteristically blunt. "Nobody ever dared to cross the line with me," she said. "I had only one unpleasant experience of being objectified by the director. I never worked with him again."

The incident she described was from the filming of Shor, in which she played a streetwalker opposite Manoj Kumar. The director wanted her to wear a ghagra-choli without a dupatta throughout the film. Jaya refused. A dispute followed. She held her ground, and that was the last time she set foot on that director's set.

Decades later, the anecdote still carries the force of a slap. Not because the industry has changed beyond recognition since — but because, as Peddi proves, it hasn't always.

Kareena's Masterclass in Classic Sensuality

Kareena Kapoor Khan took a different approach — less confrontation, more film history seminar. And she was devastating.

"Look at Kajol in that song, 'Suraj Hua Maddham' in Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham, or Srideviji in the song 'Tere Mere Honthon Pe' in Chandni — they blew the screen apart without any skin show. My mother-in-law in that song in Aradhana, 'Roop Tera Mastana', was covered from head to toe. She was the epitome of sensuality." — Kareena Kapoor Khan

The point was precise and unanswerable: Indian cinema has a century-long tradition of women commanding the screen through presence, craft, and performance. The idea that sensuality requires exposure isn't just reductive — it's historically illiterate.

Kareena didn't name Peddi directly. She didn't need to.

The Director Responded — and the Re-Edit Is Real

Buchi Babu Sana broke his silence on social media with an apology that read more like genuine reflection than crisis management. "As a filmmaker, I believe cinema should entertain, inspire, and connect with audiences," he wrote. "It should never make anyone feel uncomfortable or disrespected. We have heard the feedback regarding certain scenes in Peddi and have taken it seriously."

The confirmation: the scenes that drew the most criticism will be re-edited. Not pulled, not defended — changed. For a Telugu blockbuster mid-theatrical run, that's almost unprecedented.

Other voices joined the chorus. Nithya Menen urged actors to set boundaries on set. Dimple Hayathi defended Janhvi directly, arguing that actors shouldn't bear responsibility for choices embedded in the script. Jagapathi Babu came out in support of Janhvi amid the trolling, while Kangana Ranaut added her voice to the broader conversation about female objectification in cinema.

What This Means for NRI Audiences

For the diaspora watching from New York, London, and Toronto, this isn't just a controversy about one film. It's the clearest sign yet that Indian cinema's audience — especially its younger, globally aware audience — is no longer willing to passively consume the male gaze dressed up as entertainment. The backlash against Peddi isn't cancel culture. It's taste evolving faster than the industry's instincts.

The box office didn't punish Peddi. ₹270 crore says the film still works as spectacle. But the conversation around it may end up mattering more than the collection. When Jaya Bachchan tells you she refused to be objectified in the 1970s, and Kareena Kapoor proves that sensuality and respect were never mutually exclusive, the message is clear:

Bollywood has always known better. It just didn't always choose to act like it.
